segments.text: Everyone has opinions about AI's future, whether they're AI warriors or AI optimists.
No matter how confident those people are, some of the biggest results in any massive shift
are things no one predicted.
The best way to see it is a true story from 1902 Hanoi.
The city had a big problem.
Their new sewer system was overrun with rats.
They devised a perfect plan.
Hunters simply turn in a severed rat's tail and they collect a cash payment.
Tails poured in by the thousands.
Based strictly on the volume of tails collected, the brilliance of the plan was obvious.
The system appeared to be functioning flawlessly.
Then people saw something very strange.
Rats running around the city with no tails.
Here's what happened.
Rats can live a relatively full rat life even without their tails and keep having more rat babies.
The rat hunters came up with a clever plan to keep the tail supply strong.
They clipped the tails for the payment but let the rats live.
A dead rat pays once.
A live rat pays forever.
Some rat entrepreneurs went even further and started dedicated rat farms.
When Hanoi finally stopped the program, they had a mountain of rat tails, but more rats than when it started.
The payment system worked exactly as designed.
People delivered tails and the government paid them.
But the real goal was fewer rats and the program encouraged people to keep rats alive.
Once you see that shape, you find it everywhere.
This chart breaks down four famous plans and where each one actually landed.
SMS text messaging was originally designed as a narrow, basic service to pass short notes across mobile networks.
Those early phones were built almost entirely for voice calls.
But users took that secondary, short form feature and turned it into their primary method of communication,
creating the foundational backbone of traditional texting.
GPS was built by the US military to guide ships, aircraft and weapons.
But once available in civilian hands, human ingenuity took over.
Today, it is the invisible engine powering everyday location tools like Google Maps.
Australia imported cane toads to eat beetles destroying sugar cane.
They barely controlled the pests, poisoned native animals and spread across the country.
To ease congestion, Texas spent $2.8 billion widening Houston's Katie Freeway.
By 2014, one rush hour trip took 51% longer than it had three years earlier.
Two of these plans turned out better than anyone predicted and two turned out worse.
The biggest results were never the plan.
That last example requires a closer look.
Whitening a road seems like the obvious way to reduce traffic.
But there is a general behavioral pattern behind it.
Make a road easier to drive and more people drive it.
Trips that weren't worth making before suddenly start getting made.
The new space quickly fills back up with new drivers.
That doesn't explain the whole Houston number by itself.
Plenty else changed in those three years.
But it demonstrates why treating a complex behavioral system with a mechanical fix like
just add lanes doesn't always end congestion.
The system reacts to the new space.
Now point that history at AI.
Every AI expert, optimist, and warrior alike is making a prediction about the future.
The most important thing AI does in your lifetime, good or bad,
may be something nobody in any camp, any lab, or any course has thought of yet.
That's not a reason to fear the future.
It's the reason to walk into it curious with your eyes open.
You do not need to predict the future perfectly.
You need to recognize uncertainty, watch what people actually do,
and build skills that still matter when the forecast changes.
Some of the biggest results are the ones nobody predicted.
That's the best reason to stay curious.
